title: Faith, Love, and the Hope Stored Up
subtitle: Colossians 1:1–8
description: Paul thanks God for a church he has never met, whose faith and love grew from the hope stored up for them in heaven.
paragraphs: The letter opens the way Paul's letters do, with names and a blessing: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother,” writing to them: “To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae.” Then the greeting: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father.” What the greeting does not show is that Paul has never stood in that city. Later in this same letter he will say he is struggling for the Colossians and for all who have not met him face to face. This series places the letter with his imprisonment among the prison letters, and it comes to Colossae the way the gospel first did, carried by someone else.

Thanksgiving comes first, and it is thanks for people known only by report. “We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,” he writes, and the reason follows: “because we have heard about your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints.” Heard about is the honest phrase. Their faith and love reached Paul as news, the way his chains reached them, and the news was good enough to pray over with thanks.

Faith and love have a source, and Paul names it before he names anything else about them: “the faith and love proceeding from the hope stored up for you in heaven.” Stored up is treasure language; the hope is already kept somewhere safe, and the faith and love grow out of it here. It is not a hope they invented. It came to them in a message: “of which you have already heard in the word of truth, the gospel,” the gospel, he adds simply, “that has come to you.”

That gospel is on the move everywhere, not only in their small city. “All over the world this gospel is bearing fruit and growing, just as it has been doing among you since the day you heard it and truly understood the grace of God.” Fruit and growth are farm words, and Paul sets the Colossians' patch of ground inside a worldwide field: the same gospel, the same fruit, from the day they heard it. A young church Paul has never seen is not an outpost of something small; it is part of something already filling the world.

The man who carried it to them gets the episode's last word, because he carried their story back too. “You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf,” Paul writes, “and who also informed us of your love in the Spirit.” Epaphras is one of their own, and he is a different man from Epaphroditus, the Philippians' messenger, though the names run close. Teacher one way, reporter the other: the whole relationship between Paul and this church runs through him, and the prayer his report started comes next.

title: The Prayer That Has Not Stopped
subtitle: Colossians 1:9–14
description: Since the day he heard of them, Paul has not stopped praying that they be filled with the knowledge of God's will.
paragraphs: Epaphras brought the report, and the report started a prayer that has not let up since. “For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you,” Paul writes, and then he tells them exactly what the prayer asks: “and asking God to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding.” Not more information for its own sake. Knowledge of God's will, the kind that comes with wisdom and understanding attached, prayed down on people Paul has never met as steadily as if he lived among them.

The prayer has a purpose clause, and the purpose is a walk: “so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God.” Walk is Paul's everyday word for a whole life lived out step by step. Fruit again, as in the first episode's worldwide field, and growth again, but now the growth is in knowing God himself, the knowledge circling back richer than the knowledge prayed for.

Strength comes next, and it is aimed at endurance, not escape. They are to be strengthened, he prays, “being strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience, and joyfully” doing the thing that closes the prayer's long sentence: “giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light.” Qualified is the surprise word. Nobody qualifies themselves for an inheritance; it comes by birth or by gift. Saints in the light have a share kept for them, and the Father has already made them fit to receive it.

How did people in darkness come to hold a share in the light? Paul answers with a rescue told in two moves: “He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son.” Rescued out of one dominion, brought into another kingdom, and the kingdom belongs to a Son described by his belovedness before anything else about him is said. Darkness here is not a mood; it is a ruling power, and the transfer out of it is already done.

The prayer lands on the Son and stays there: “in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.” Redemption is a buying-back word, and Paul defines it on the spot as forgiveness, trespasses wiped clean. Fourteen verses into the letter, everything has been aimed at this person: the hope stored up, the fruit growing, the rescue accomplished. Now Paul turns and looks at him directly, and what comes next is the highest passage in the letter.

title: The Image of the Invisible God
subtitle: Colossians 1:15–23
description: The great hymn to the Son: image of the invisible God, creator of all things, head of the church, reconciler through his cross.
paragraphs: The prayer ends looking at the Son, and now Paul lets the looking become a hymn. It begins with visibility: “The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation.” God cannot be seen; the Son is his image, the unseen made seen. Firstborn here stands where Paul puts it, at the head of the sentence about creation, and the next lines explain the ground it stands on rather than shrinking it.

Creation itself is the ground. “For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities.” Nothing is left outside the list, including every rank of power that human beings or angels could name. Then the direction of it: “All things were created through Him and for Him.” And before any of it stood, he was: “He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.” The one through whom everything was made is also the one keeping everything from flying apart.

The hymn turns from creation to the church without changing its tune. “And He is the head of the body, the church; He is the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence.” Firstborn sounds a second time, now over the dead and rising. The reason for the height is stated plainly: “For God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him.” Not a portion of God parceled out. All his fullness, dwelling in this one person, because God was pleased to have it so.

Fullness that dwells is fullness that reconciles: “and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross.” The scope is as wide as the creation list was: all things, earth and heaven together. And the means is not force but blood, peace made at a cross. The hymn that began with thrones and dominions ends at an execution, and it treats the execution as the place where the universe's peace was settled.

Then the hymn comes home to its readers, and Paul will not let them hold it at arm's length. “Once you were alienated from God and were hostile in your minds, engaging in evil deeds.” That was once. “But now He has reconciled you by Christ’s physical body through death,” he writes, “to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence.” The condition he adds is a staying, not a striving: “if indeed you continue in your faith, established and firm, not moved from the hope of the gospel you heard, which has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven, and of which I, Paul, have become a servant.” The servant of that gospel is the man writing, and his service is the next thing the letter explains.

title: Christ in You, the Hope of Glory
subtitle: Colossians 1:24–2:5
description: Paul's sufferings, his commission, and the mystery hidden for ages and now revealed: Christ in you, the hope of glory.
paragraphs: Paul calls himself the gospel's servant, and the first thing he says about the service is that suffering belongs to it and he is glad. “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church.” The sentence stands as he wrote it, strange and unsoftened: the chained apostle rejoicing, his own flesh carrying affliction on behalf of a body of people that includes a church he has never seen.

His authority for it is a commission, not an ambition. “I became its servant by the commission God gave me to fully proclaim to you the word of God,” he writes, and the word he was commissioned to proclaim carries something once kept back: “the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints.” Hidden through ages and generations of God's own people, and now, in Paul's lifetime, opened. A mystery in his letters is not a puzzle to solve but a secret God kept until the moment he chose to tell it.

And the secret, when told, is a sentence a reader can hold in one hand: “To them God has chosen to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.” Among the Gentiles is the scandal inside the glory: the kept-back secret turns out to be Christ dwelling in people who were outside. What Paul does with it is proclaim: “We proclaim Him, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ.” The labor runs on borrowed power: “To this end I also labor, striving with all His energy working powerfully within me.”

That labor reaches past the churches he founded to this one he did not. “For I want you to know how much I am struggling for you and for those at Laodicea, and for all who have not met me face to face,” he tells them, and the struggle has faces in view: “that they may be encouraged in heart, knit together in love, and filled with the full riches of complete understanding, so that they may know the mystery of God, namely Christ.” The mystery has a name, and the name is a person, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” Hidden again, but hidden the way treasure is hidden in a field: in one known place, waiting to be dug up.

Why say all this to a church doing well? Because someone may come talking. “I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric,” Paul writes, and the sentence is the hinge of the whole letter: the warning begins here, inside the encouragement. Absence does not weaken his claim on them: “For although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I delight to see your orderly condition and firm faith in Christ.” Delight first, then defense. The letter now turns to guard the ground it has just celebrated.

title: Rooted and Built Up in Him
subtitle: Colossians 2:6–15
description: Walk as you received him, beware captivity through empty deception, and see the debt nailed to the cross.
paragraphs: The defense begins with a command to keep going exactly as they started. “Therefore, just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him,” Paul writes, and he piles three pictures on top of each other to say what the walking looks like: “rooted and built up in Him, established in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness.” Rooted is a tree. Built up is a building. Established is a legal word, something confirmed and made firm. All three say the same thing three ways: stay where you were planted, and let the growth come from there.

The threat is named as a kidnapping. “See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, which are based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ.” Captive is war language, a prisoner carried off. The weapon is talk: philosophy, deception Paul calls empty, tradition that traces back to human beings and to the world's spiritual forces. He does not name the teachers behind it, here or anywhere in the letter, and neither does this telling. What he sets against the empty talk is fullness.

The fullness is in Christ, bodily. “For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form.” And because it dwells there, something has already happened to them: “And you have been made complete in Christ, who is the head over every ruler and authority.” Complete is the word to hold onto. A people being told they lack something, some extra step or secret, are answered by a finished fact: you have been made complete in the one who heads every ruler and authority there is.

Their own history with him is told as burial and resurrection. “In Him you were also circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature, with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands.” Then the water: “And having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead.” The past tense runs through it all, done things, and its hardest case is the one Paul states next: “When you were dead in your trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your sinful nature, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our trespasses.” Dead people do not rescue themselves. God made them alive, and the making alive and the forgiving are the same act.

What happened to their record is the letter's boldest picture, a debt document “having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross!” Nailed up in public, the way such records were displayed for everyone to see. And the powers that might have enforced it fare no better: “And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.” Disarmed, paraded, triumphed over, by the cross of all instruments. The warning's second half now turns from captivity to judgment, and it is gentler only in tone.

title: Shadows, Not the Body
subtitle: Colossians 2:16–23
description: Let no one judge or disqualify you: these things are a shadow, and the body that casts it belongs to Christ.
paragraphs: After the cross's triumph, the small courts lose their authority. “Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath.” Menus and calendars are the battleground named: food, drink, festivals, monthly and weekly holy days. Paul does not argue that the days were nothing. He argues from what a shadow is: “These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.” A shadow is real, and it is cast by something realer. Chase the body, not its outline on the ground.

A second court disqualifies on spiritual experience instead. “Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you with speculation about what he has seen.” Visions claimed, humility performed, angels worshiped: the package presents itself as deeper religion. Paul's verdict runs the other way: “Such a person is puffed up without basis by his unspiritual mind.” And the diagnosis underneath it is disconnection: “He has lost connection to the head, from whom the whole body, supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows as God causes it to grow.” A body grows from its head or it does not grow at all.

Then Paul asks the question the whole warning has been building toward. “If you have died with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its regulations:” Death is the premise. They have died with Christ to the very forces the regulations claim to manage, so living under the regulations means behaving as if the death never happened. What follows the colon is the regulations' own voice, quoted so the readers can hear how it sounds from outside.

The voice is all prohibitions: “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!” Touch nothing, taste nothing, handle nothing, as if holiness were a matter of keeping hands clean of ordinary things. Paul answers with the things' own shelf life: “These will all perish with use, because they are based on human commands and teachings.” The rules guard things that perish in the using, and their authority is human all the way down: commands and teachings of men, dressed as the commands of God.

He grants the package its one true claim before he closes the case. “Such restrictions indeed have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-prescribed worship, their false humility, and their harsh treatment of the body; but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.” Appearance of wisdom, he allows. Self-prescribed worship, humility as a show, severity toward the body: it all looks like the serious path. But a fence around the body does nothing against the desires it was built to starve. The warning ends, and the letter turns from what to refuse to what to wear.

title: Put Off, Put On
subtitle: Colossians 3:1–11
description: Raised with Christ, put to death the earthly nature, take off the old self, and put on the new.
paragraphs: The new life starts from a finished fact and a direction. “Therefore, since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.” Raised already, past tense, and the striving runs upward toward a person seated in honor. The mind gets the same marching orders as the life: “Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things.” The reason underneath is a death and a hiding: “For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God.” Hidden the way the treasures were hidden in Christ earlier in the letter, kept in a known and safe place. And the hiding has an end date: “When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory.”

Because of where they now live, some things get executed. “Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed, which is idolatry.” The list runs from acts to appetites and lands on greed, which Paul flatly renames: wanting more is a form of worship, aimed at the wrong god. The stakes are not private: “Because of these, the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.” Nor is this aimed at strangers. “When you lived among them, you also used to walk in these ways.” Used to. The old walk is named as a former address.

A second list covers the social sins, the ones that come out of the mouth and the temper. “But now you must put aside all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips.” Anger heating into rage, rage curdling into malice, malice talking. Then truth-telling between believers gets its own command: “Do not lie to one another, since you have taken off the old self with its practices.” Taken off is clothing language, and the whole rest of the letter runs on it. The old self is not improved or patched. It is removed, practices and all, like a garment that no longer belongs on the body.

What replaces it is also worn: “and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator.” Being renewed is present tense, still happening: the new self grows toward the image of the one who made it, knowledge deepening the resemblance. The image language reaches back to the hymn's opening, the Son who is the image of the invisible God. Renewal here is a person being remade in knowledge after the pattern of that image.

A new humanity wears this self, and its census is unlike any other. “Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all.” Nations, religious marks, cultures from the center of the map to its wildest edge, the owned and the free: the old categories are not balanced against each other, they are gone, replaced by a single fact stated twice for emphasis. Christ is all, and Christ is in all. What this people wears together is the next thing Paul describes.

title: Clothe Yourselves with Love
subtitle: Colossians 3:12–4:1
description: Compassion, kindness, and love over all, then the teaching walks into the household and addresses everyone in it.
paragraphs: The clothing metaphor turns from removal to dressing, and the wardrobe is a character. “Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience.” Elect, holy, beloved: the names come before the outfit, identity first and dress second. The daily friction of shared life is planned for, not wished away: “Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.” The measure of their forgiving is someone else's forgiving of them. And one garment goes over everything: “And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity.” Love as the belt or the outer coat, the piece that holds all the others together.

Peace and the word take up residence together. “Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. And be thankful.” Rule is an umpire's word; the peace of Christ arbitrates inside them. Then the teaching life: “Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God.” Richly is the measure, a word well stocked, and it comes out as teaching and as singing in the same breath. The summary of the whole section fits in one verse: “And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him.”

Then the teaching walks into the house, and it speaks to everyone in it by name, in both directions. To wives first: “Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.” To husbands, a command about love and a prohibition about tone: “Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them.” To children: “Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord.” And to fathers, a warning about the damage a parent can do by pressure: “Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged.” Submission, love, obedience, restraint: each member of the household is addressed as a person who answers to the Lord directly, and the stronger party in each pair is the one told to hold back.

Slaves are addressed the same way, as workers whose real audience is not human. “Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, not only to please them while they are watching, but with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord.” The reason reframes all work, theirs and everyone's since: “Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for men,” and the wage is restated too: “because you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving.” Justice stands behind the whole table: “Whoever does wrong will be repaid for his wrong, and there is no favoritism.”

The table's last word crosses into the next chapter and lands on the powerful. “Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven.” Also is the leveling word. The man with slaves of his own has a Master of his own, and what is right and fair is owed downward because it is watched from above. The household teaching ends with heaven looking into the house, and the letter turns outward, to prayer and to the people outside the house entirely.

title: Remember My Chains
subtitle: Colossians 4:2–18
description: Prayer for a door for the word, the carriers and greetings, the Laodicea exchange, and Paul's own-hand close.
paragraphs: The letter's last movement opens with an order about prayer that could stand over the whole book. “Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful,” he writes, “as you pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains.” The chained man does not ask them to pray the chains off. He asks for a door for the word, an opening to speak the mystery that put him in chains, and for his own clarity in speaking it: “Pray that I may declare it clearly, as I should.” Then the direction turns outward: “Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time.” And their speech gets its seasoning: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.”

The news of Paul himself travels by person, not by letter. “Tychicus will tell you all the news about me. He is a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant in the Lord.” The same Tychicus who carried Ephesians carries this letter too, sent, Paul says, “I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts.” Beside him travels a Colossian going home: “With him I am sending Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you about everything here.” Faithful and beloved is all this letter says of Onesimus. The other half of his errand belongs to the next letter in this series, the short one that bears his story, and it is left there.

The greetings begin with the prisoners and the family connections. “My fellow prisoner Aristarchus sends you greetings, as does Mark the cousin of Barnabas.” Mark comes with a standing instruction Paul expects them to remember: “You have already received instructions about him: If he comes to you, welcome him.” Then a man most readers know only by his other name: “Jesus, who is called Justus, also sends greetings.” Paul sums this small company with unusual warmth: “These are the only Jews among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.” Few, Jewish, fellow workers, a comfort: the greetings keep being miniature portraits.

Epaphras gets the fullest portrait of all, and it is a portrait of prayer. “Epaphras, who is one of you and a servant of Christ Jesus, sends you greetings. He is always wrestling in prayer for you, so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God.” The man who first carried the gospel to Colossae now wrestles for it at a distance, and Paul testifies for him like a witness: “For I testify about him that he goes to great pains for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis.” Two more names close the greetings from Paul's side: “Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas send you greetings.” And greetings flow back the other way too: “Greet the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha and the church that meets at her house.”

The letter's last instructions send it traveling and land one charge on one man. “After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.” Another letter existed, written to Laodicea, and the Colossians were to read it; what it said is not known from this one, and this telling invents nothing about it. Then the charge: “See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord,” spoken to Archippus, and left there, with no story attached. And Paul takes the pen himself for the close: “This greeting is in my own hand.” The signature is also the reminder: “Remember my chains. Grace be with you.”
